blocks.text: A catalytic converter is a ceramic or metallic monolith with a honeycomb-like structure (Figure 12.6). Its inner channels carry a layer of alumina to provide a high surface area, and the expensive noble metals platinum, palladium and rhodium are dispersed on the alumina. These metals catalyse three redox reactions that remove the harmful exhaust gases: the three-way converter converts harmful CO, NO and hydrocarbons into CO2, N2 and water. The precious metals can be recycled. Reduction: 2NO(g) + 2CO(g) over Pt/Rh gives N2(g) + 2CO2(g). Oxidation: 2CO(g) + O2(g) over Pt/Rh gives 2CO2(g), and C2H4 + 3O2 gives 2CO2 + 2H2O (printed as 2C2H4 + 6O2 giving 4CO2 + 4H2O).

blocks.prompt: What is the basic principle of a catalytic converter, and do hybrid and electric cars have them (Quick Check 12.3b, c)?
blocks.explanation: Hot exhaust passes over a huge surface of platinum, palladium and rhodium on alumina in a honeycomb; the metals catalyse the reduction of NO by CO to nitrogen and the oxidation of CO and unburnt hydrocarbons to CO2 and water, without being consumed. Hybrid cars still burn petrol, so they have converters; fully electric cars have no engine exhaust and so need none.

items: Honeycomb monolith, alumina washcoat, Pt/Pd/Rh; three redox reactions: 2NO + 2CO to N2 + 2CO2 (reduction), 2CO + O2 to 2CO2 and C2H4 + 3O2 to 2CO2 + 2H2O (oxidation); metals recyclable.
